task.description: WF-03 Step 3b: SECURITY-REVIEWER gate on ISS-0418's InvocationLease change. Run scope test against git diff main...HEAD, apply INV-1..INV-9 per security-invariants.md, and separately assess (1) whether the underlying multi-tenant availability hazard this design accepts as unfixed needs recording as a durable accepted risk, (2) whether InvocationLease itself is a DoS surface (unbounded growth, cap exhaustion, crash fail-open/fail-closed correctness), and (3) whether the moduledoc truthfully states that production dispatch does not call this module.

result.summary:
SCOPE TEST: OUT OF SCOPE on the canonical list. Verified via `git diff main...HEAD --name-only`: the diff touches lib/letflow/design/iss0418-wasm-concurrency-cap.md (design doc), lib/letflow/engine/wasm/invocation_lease.ex (new GenServer), lib/letflow/supervisor/infrastructure.ex (adds it as child 11/18), three test files (call_timeout_test.exs, host_api_write_test.exs, plugin_handler_test.exs -- wiring only), a new test file (invocation_lease_test.exs), and handoffs/registry.json bookkeeping. Confirmed directly, not inferred from the handoff's own claim: `git diff main...HEAD -- lib/letflow/engine/wasm/plugin_handler.ex lib/letflow/engine/plugin_interface.ex` returns EMPTY, and `grep -rn 'try_acquire|InvocationLease' lib/` finds zero hits outside the three files already named (design doc, invocation_lease.ex, infrastructure.ex) -- i.e. no production dispatch call site invokes this module. No API route, migration, secret-resolution, response-shaping, or lookup-by-ID path is added or modified. Recorded explicitly per the role file: out of scope -- no tenant-data path touched.

=== INV-1..INV-9 applicability ===
INV-1 (tenant data isolation): NOT-APPLICABLE. No Ecto schema, migration, or query added/changed. `priv/repo/migrations/` diff is empty (confirmed: `git diff main...HEAD --name-only | grep migrations` -> no output). InvocationLease holds only in-memory GenServer state (cap/in_use/leases keyed by monitor ref and pid) -- no persistence, no tenant_id, no :prefix concern.
INV-2 (server-side field authorisation): NOT-APPLICABLE -- no API response type touched, and still pre-S4.
INV-3 (untrusted runtime sandboxing): NOT-APPLICABLE as a WASM-sandboxing-capability change -- this module does not touch the sandbox's capability allowlist or host-function surface; it only bounds how many invocations may run concurrently. Still pre-S5's own decision record for the sandboxing invariant itself, so also not yet live on its own terms.
INV-4 (secrets by reference only): APPLIES (live). Verified: `grep -rn "System.get_env" ...` finds no hits in the new files (none needed -- config key is `Application.get_env(:letflow, :invocation_lease, [])[:cap]`, a plain integer, not a secret). Heuristic hardcoded-secret grep against invocation_lease.ex and infrastructure.ex returns zero matches. PASS.
INV-5 (not-found/forbidden indistinguishability): NOT-APPLICABLE -- no lookup-by-ID endpoint, pre-S4.
INV-6 (new data-access paths prove scoping): NOT-APPLICABLE as a data-access-path invariant -- InvocationLease is not a data-access path (no tenant business data read or written). This handoff itself satisfies INV-6's meta-requirement (a SECURITY-REVIEWER pass exists, explicitly enumerating INV-1..INV-9).
INV-7 (no SQL string interpolation): APPLIES (live, Ecto in use elsewhere). Verified: `grep -n "Repo.query" lib/letflow/engine/wasm/invocation_lease.ex lib/letflow/supervisor/infrastructure.ex` -> zero hits. PASS (trivially -- no SQL of any kind in this diff).
INV-8 (no unhandled crashes on realistic failure paths): APPLIES (live). Verified: heuristic `grep -n "^\s*{:ok, .*} = "` against invocation_lease.ex -> zero hits. Manually read the full module (both handle_call clauses and handle_info/2): try_acquire's capacity check is a plain boolean guard with no raise path; release/1 uses Map.pop and pattern-matches both {nil, _} and {%{...}, _} exhaustively, so an unknown/already-released/hand-constructed lease id cannot crash the GenServer (documented idempotent no-op); the :DOWN handler uses Enum.find and pattern-matches both nil and {id, _entry}, so a stale :DOWN for an already-demonitored ref cannot crash it either. No external I/O, no tenant-controlled input reaches this module in this diff (it is called only from test code and, in future, would receive no tenant data itself -- it takes no arguments from the caller other than an opaque, self-issued Lease struct). PASS.
INV-9 (tenant-controlled outbound URL validation): NOT-APPLICABLE -- no outbound HTTP request of any kind in this diff.

=== ENGAGED FINDING 1: the underlying availability hazard is real, correctly NOT claimed fixed, and the current record of it is adequate but should be watched ===
ISSUE-FIXER's diagnosis (live-verified against wasmex's Rust source, reproduced on-host: 16 concurrent hangs exhaust a node-global TOKIO_RUNTIME, zero recovery observed after 90s) establishes a genuine cross-tenant availability hazard: one tenant's hung WASM plugin permanently consumes a slot in a pool shared by every tenant on that node, with no in-BEAM reclamation. This is squarely the kind of concern INV-1's own spirit (isolation) and INV-8's own spirit (one tenant's malformed/misbehaving input must not degrade others) exist to catch, even though neither invariant's letter names 'shared native thread pool starvation' specifically -- INV-1 is about query-level tenant_id scoping and INV-8 is about BEAM-process crashes, not this exact resource-exhaustion shape. I am not finding a BLOCKER against either invariant's letter, because this diff does not worsen the hazard (production dispatch is unchanged, byte-for-byte, per the confirmed-empty diff above) -- but flagging that the pipeline currently has no invariant that names 'shared-runtime resource exhaustion across tenants' as its own numbered rule, which is a gap worth closing given this is now an eleven-plus-recurrence, MAJOR-severity, load-bearing issue. On the specific question asked -- is shipping a TEST-ONLY cap while leaving PRODUCTION uncapped an acceptable posture, or does it need recording somewhere more durable than a design doc -- my assessment: the design doc plus the moduledoc plus ISS-0418.yaml's own eleven-plus-recurrence history is already a reasonably durable, cross-referenced record (design doc found via moduledoc, issue found via design doc, both survive independently of this run's own handoffs), and the ORCH decision log at design doc §10 ('OQ-E RESOLUTION') already states plainly that ISS-0418 stays OPEN and that production is not capped. This is adequate as an interim record. It is NOT adequate as a permanent state: I recommend (non-blocking, MINOR, per 'No Issue Left Local-Only') that ORCH ensure a follow-up requirement exists (OQ-C in the design doc names REQ-056 as the most plausible dispatch-integration target) is tracked in docs/requirements.yaml or the issue queue with a status that is visibly not 'someday' -- e.g. confirm REQ-056 is not blocked/deprioritized in a way that lets this sit uncapped in production indefinitely while the CI-flake framing keeps the urgency artificially scoped to 'test suite reliability' rather than 'production tenant-isolation gap.' This is a process recommendation, not a code defect, and does not block this diff.

=== ENGAGED FINDING 2: InvocationLease itself is not a new DoS surface, and its crash behaviour is correct (fails open) ===
Read the full module (lib/letflow/engine/wasm/invocation_lease.ex). Assessed each named risk:
  (a) Unbounded state growth from monitors: NO. `leases` map is bounded by `cap` (a fixed positive integer read once at init) -- try_acquire refuses to insert once `in_use >= cap`, so the map can never exceed `cap` entries. Not attacker-growable beyond the configured cap regardless of caller behaviour.
  (b) A caller that acquires and never releases: HANDLED, by design, via the monitor. try_acquire/1 monitors the acquiring pid at acquisition time; if that process dies without calling release/1 (including via Task.shutdown(:brutal_kill), the exact scenario ISSUE-FIXER's diagnosis identifies as the reason Letflow.Admission was unsuitable unmodified), handle_info({:DOWN,...}) decrements in_use and frees the slot automatically. This directly closes the 'never-released ref' problem ISSUE-FIXER flagged against reusing Admission as-is (diagnosis §2, Option A) -- confirmed as an actual implemented mechanism, not merely asserted: the code monitors `elem(from, 0)` (the GenServer.call caller pid), not `self()` inside handle_call/3, which is the correct pid to monitor. A caller that never releases only ties up its slot for as long as that caller process itself stays alive; once the caller dies (which it must, eventually, on any real BEAM process, including via its own supervisor's crash handling), the slot recovers. This is a materially different, better failure mode than Letflow.Admission's own documented 'stays counted until this process itself restarts or the ref is explicitly released' semantics for a caller that never dies but also never releases -- not applicable to today's diff since nothing production calls this yet, but relevant to flag for whoever designs the future production call site: the guarantee is 'recovers when the CALLER dies,' not 'recovers when the underlying WASM hang resolves' (it never does, per Finding 1) -- so a long-lived production caller that acquires a lease, dispatches a hang, and then (correctly, per its own timeout logic) gives up and moves on to handle other invocations without itself dying, MUST still call release/1 on the timeout path for the slot to free promptly; the monitor is a backstop for caller death, not a substitute for a correct release-on-every-path implementation. The design doc (§8.1, not fully quoted in my required reading but referenced throughout §0/§10) and the moduledoc's own 'What this module DOES guarantee' section correctly scope this as bounding concurrent callers, not reclaiming native leaks -- consistent with this.
  (c) Cap exhaustion wedging legitimate callers: NO persistent wedge. try_acquire/1 is synchronous and non-queuing -- it returns {:error, :capacity} immediately rather than blocking a caller indefinitely, so a caller that is refused admission is never itself blocked/wedged by this module; it is the caller's own responsibility (unchanged, since nothing calls this today) to decide what to do with {:error, :capacity} (e.g. reject or queue at a higher layer). Given (b)'s monitor-backed auto-release, exhaustion is also not permanent: it recovers as soon as enough acquiring processes die, bounded by ordinary process churn, not stuck forever the way the underlying native leak is.
  Crash behaviour of the GenServer itself: verified fail-open, and correct for this use case. On InvocationLease's own crash/restart, init/1 resets to in_use: 0, leases: %{} -- i.e. a crash of the semaphore process ITSELF widens admission (fails open) rather than wedging it shut (fail closed). This is the right direction for an availability-focused harm-reduction gate: failing open on the gate's own crash means a bug in InvocationLease cannot itself become a new denial-of-service vector that blocks all WASM dispatch; it only transiently loses the admission-count property, which is explicitly documented in the moduledoc as an accepted, deliberate tradeoff mirroring Letflow.Admission's own precedent. I agree this is correct: an admission gate whose own failure mode is 'now nothing can run' would be a strictly worse availability posture than the uncapped status quo it's meant to improve on.
  Overall: InvocationLease does not introduce a new DoS surface. It only reduces exposure (bounds simultaneous blast radius, per its own honestly-scoped claim) and its own failure modes are self-limiting (bounded state, non-blocking refusal, fail-open crash recovery).

=== ENGAGED FINDING 3: moduledoc is truthful, verified word-for-word against the actual (non-)wiring ===
Read lib/letflow/engine/wasm/invocation_lease.ex's @moduledoc in full. It states, in bold, up front (second paragraph): 'PRODUCTION WASM DISPATCH DOES NOT CALL THIS MODULE YET, STATED AS PLAINLY AS THE NATIVE-LEAK LIMITATION BELOW' followed by an explicit list of what is NOT modified (PluginInterface.invoke/2,3, PluginHandler) and the consequence ('A real WASM guest invocation reached by production dispatch is therefore admitted with NO cap of any kind today'). I verified this claim is true, not merely present: (1) `git diff main...HEAD -- lib/letflow/engine/wasm/plugin_handler.ex lib/letflow/engine/plugin_interface.ex` is empty -- byte-for-byte unmodified; (2) `grep -rn 'try_acquire|InvocationLease' lib/` finds no call site in either file, or anywhere in lib/ outside the design doc, invocation_lease.ex itself, and infrastructure.ex's supervision wiring. The supervisor comment at the InvocationLease child-spec entry in infrastructure.ex independently repeats the same claim ('NOTHING in production dispatch calls try_acquire/0 yet -- only the :wasm_hang test suite does'), consistent with the moduledoc. A future maintainer reading only invocation_lease.ex's moduledoc (without the design doc) would correctly conclude production is unprotected -- the moduledoc does not merely disclaim liability in passing, it leads with this fact in bold before describing what the module does guarantee, which is the right ordering to prevent exactly the false-confidence failure mode this finding was checking for. PASS -- no discrepancy found between claim and code.

=== Overall verdict ===
STATUS: PASS. Out of scope on the canonical tenant-data-path list (confirmed by scope test, not assumed). All applicable invariants (INV-4, INV-7, INV-8) verified PASS by direct grep and manual code read; INV-1/2/3/5/9 correctly NOT-APPLICABLE and confirmed by diff inspection, not by default assumption. The three engaged concerns are resolved: (1) the availability hazard is real and unfixed, but this diff does not worsen it and the design/moduledoc/issue chain records it adequately for now -- a non-blocking process recommendation is filed below to keep the follow-up (dispatch-integration requirement, e.g. REQ-056) visible rather than let CI-flake framing understate it as production risk; (2) InvocationLease is not itself a DoS surface -- bounded state, non-blocking refusal, monitor-backed auto-release closing the brutal-kill leak class, fail-open crash recovery, all verified against the actual code, not assumed from the design doc's claims; (3) the moduledoc is truthful and verified against the real (non-)wiring, not merely well-written.

issues.finding: The multi-tenant availability hazard this design's own diagnosis confirms (one tenant's hung WASM plugin permanently starves a node-global thread pool shared by every tenant) remains completely unmitigated in production after this merge -- by design and correctly disclosed, not a defect in this diff. The risk is currently recorded only in a design doc, a module's own moduledoc, and an issue file framed primarily around CI flakiness. Recommend ORCH confirm the future dispatch-integration requirement named in the design doc (OQ-C, most plausibly REQ-056) is actually tracked with visible priority in docs/requirements.yaml, not left to age indefinitely under a 'test suite reliability' framing that understates it as a production tenant-isolation exposure. Non-blocking -- this is a process/tracking recommendation, not a finding against this diff's own invariant compliance.

result.next_action: Return to ORCH. SECURITY-REVIEWER gate PASSES for this diff (out of scope on the canonical tenant-data-path list; all applicable invariants verified). One MINOR process recommendation filed (follow-up requirement visibility) -- does not block merge.
